title: Soil Holds: Matter, Memory, Commons
summary: A proposal for Angel’s Knoll connects soil repair, urban memory, and community stewardship through an accessible landscape shaped by ongoing care.
description: Bunker Hill was cut down to build a city, and what remains is soil. The soil at Angel’s Knoll has outlasted every attempt to erase, stabilize, and pave around it. Damaged and compacted, this persistent ground forms the project’s foundation, treated as living matter, relationship, and memory.

As matter, the hill operates as a dynamic, heterogeneous field, spanning flat plateaus, sharp inclines, and shifting solar exposures. Here, site clearing initiates a material metabolism: organic debris is cycled upward to nourish preserved vegetation at the crest, while descending the slope, the physical reshaping intensifies. The ground fractures into a textured patchwork of micro-conditions, secured by varied erosion controls. Native bands bind the ground between open plots left to succeed on their own, where the slow labor of becoming soil stays in view. This is provisional ground, built without knowing the outcome and left to inherit its form.

This ongoing repair also catalyzes social connection. Occupying a sharp urban threshold between the elevated corporate plateau and historic downtown, the reconstructed soil bridges contrasting realities. We treat the balance between ecological labor and public life as an evolving relationship. Initially, the hill serves as an exposed working ground, inviting the city to work and witness the labor of rebuilding. Over time, soil rebuilding softens into everyday, recreational stewardship; observation matures into active belonging as surrounding communities merge with the site’s ongoing care—bringing compost, tending trees, and gathering seeds to disperse its renewed vitality.

Operating as memory, the hill reveals a composite of deep geology and urban remains. Miocene marine sedimentary rock, fragments of old retaining walls, and Alberhill fire clay bricks are daylighted across the landscape. These displaced remnants of Bunker Hill form a mosaic where erased history resurfaces. Yet, collective memory demands equal access. The steep incline is sculpted into a choreographed terrain. By supporting climbing, descending, perching, and gathering, the design transforms an impassable barrier into an inclusive landscape—allowing all bodies to navigate, rest within, and inhabit the city’s layered ground.
